## Motivation

The first ten vignettes worked with a handful of named states and exact probabilities.
Most models are not like that. Their uncertain parameters are continuous, a belief about
them is a set of **draws** (from a posterior, or from an elicited prior), and the model
is a simulator that returns a different outcome each time it is run.

This vignette takes a decision problem from a simulator to a decision in four steps:

1. a `SampleBelief`: draws of named parameters, with weights;
2. an `OutcomeTable`: what the model produced for every draw, action and replicate;
3. a utility counted in animals, which turns outcomes into a `PayoffTable` whose Monte
   Carlo standard errors are kept in a separate field;
4. the rules and the value of information of the earlier vignettes, now as
   **estimates**, each reported with its standard error.

**All numbers are illustrative.** The model is a toy, and its parameter values are not
estimates for any real species or site.

## The problem

A fungal skin disease has reached a pond of newts. One infected animal has been found.
The manager can mount one intervention, in week 3, or none:

- `none`: no intervention, the baseline;
- `treat`: catch 70% of the newts and bathe them in an antifungal. An infected newt is
  cured; handling kills 8% of the animals caught;
- `remove`: catch 70% of the newts and remove those that test positive: every infected
  newt caught and, through false positives, 12% of the uninfected ones.

Three things are uncertain: the weekly transmission rate (`contact`), the number of
newts in the pond (`newts`), and whether the pond is open or shaded (`habitat`; warm
water in an open pond clears infections faster).

## The model and the four adapter verbs

`DecisionAnalysis.jl` never looks inside a model. It reaches it through four verbs,
which a model package (or, here, a script) gives methods for:

| verb | meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `with_parameters(prob, θ)` | the problem with its uncertain parameters set to one draw |
| `apply_action(prob, a)` | the problem under an intervention |
| `simulate(prob; rng)` | one run, with every random number taken from `rng` |
| `outcome(solution)` | the named outcomes of the run, as counts |

The toy model is in `vignettes/_toy_pond.jl`, shared with the next two vignettes:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
using DecisionAnalysis
using Random: Xoshiro
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))
include(joinpath("..", "_toy_pond.jl"))
println("```julia\n", read(joinpath("..", "_toy_pond.jl"), String), "```")
```

Outcomes are counts of animals. No utility has been applied yet, and no cost appears
anywhere: this package counts individuals, never money.

## A sample belief

A `SampleBelief` is a table of draws, one row per draw and one column per named
parameter, with weights. Equal weights are the default and are held exactly, as
`1 // n`.

```{julia}
draws = toy_draws(Xoshiro(11), 300)
belief = SampleBelief(draws)
```

```{julia}
md_table(["draw", "contact", "newts", "habitat", "weight"],
         [[s, draws.contact[i], draws.newts[i], draws.habitat[i],
           exact(probabilities(belief)[i])] for (i, s) in enumerate(state_labels(belief)[1:5])];
         digits=3)
```

Weights need not be equal. A weighted sample has fewer effective draws than rows:

```{julia}
weighted = SampleBelief((; contact=[0.2, 0.5, 0.9], weight=[1, 1, 6]); weights=:weight)
(probabilities(weighted), effective_sample_size(weighted))
```

## An outcome table

`outcomes` runs the model over draws × actions × replicates. Each draw is propagated on
its own; the mean of the parameters is never plugged in.

```{julia}
table = outcomes(ToyPond(), TOY_ACTIONS, belief; replicates=20, seed=2026)
```

```{julia}
run_counts(table)
```

The `seed` is required. The run of replicate `r` at draw `d` gets a generator whose seed
depends on `(seed, d, r)` and **not on the action**: these are common random numbers.
Two actions in the same cell see the same epidemic up to week 3, so their difference is
not blurred by luck. The achieved correlation of the simulation noise between actions
says how well this worked:

```{julia}
alive = IndividualsUtility(:alive)
crn_correlation(table, alive)
```

A simulator that draws from one stream in event order loses this correlation once the
runs diverge. An individual-based model keeps it longer by giving every individual its
own stream derived from `rng`.

### From a table of runs

Runs made elsewhere go in directly. Any table with one row per run will do; the
keywords name its columns. A run with a failing status is **kept and counted**, never
silently dropped, and is left out of the means.

```{julia}
runs = [(; point=d, arm=a, rep=r, status=(d == 2 && a == "treat" && r == 3) ? "timeout" : "ok",
         alive=40 + 5d + 3 * (a == "treat") + r) for d in 1:3 for a in ("none", "treat") for r in 1:4]
precomputed = OutcomeTable(runs; draw=:point, action=:arm, replicate=:rep,
                           outcomes=[:alive], status=:status)
```

```{julia}
failed_runs(precomputed)
```

## Utilities counted in animals

A utility maps the outcomes of one run to a number. Three are shown here.

- `IndividualsUtility(:alive)`: every surviving newt counts, infected or not.
- `InfectionUtility(; weight=0)`: only uninfected newts count.
- `InfectionUtility(; weight=1)`: uninfected minus infected. An infected survivor is
  set against an uninfected one, because it is a source of further infection.

Whether an infected but living animal counts towards the population is a modelling
choice. It is stated here, and the weight on infected animals is swept below.

`payoff_table` applies the utility to every run and averages inside each cell, so a
cell holds a **conditional expected utility**. The standard error of each cell is kept
in its own field and is never folded into the payoff.

```{julia}
payoff = payoff_table(table, alive)
md_table(["action", "payoff at draw 1", "standard error", "payoff at draw 2", "standard error"],
         [[a, Float64(payoff.Q[i, 1]), payoff.standard_errors[i, 1], Float64(payoff.Q[i, 2]),
           payoff.standard_errors[i, 2]] for (i, a) in enumerate(action_labels(payoff))])
```

With one run per cell there is nothing to average. The table is then flagged, and no
standard error is invented:

```{julia}
one_run = outcomes(ToyPond(), TOY_ACTIONS, belief; replicates=1, seed=2026)
flagged = payoff_table(one_run, alive)
(single_replicate(flagged), flagged.standard_errors === nothing)
```

A flagged table holds single outcomes, not conditional expectations. Every maximum
taken over it is a maximum over noise, so the best reported value and the value with
information are each too high.

## The decision

```{julia}
problem = DecisionProblem(table, alive; baseline=:none)
```

Expected utility is now an estimate. `expected_utility_estimates` gives it with two
errors: the standard error when the draws are a random sample of the belief, and the
part that comes from the simulator alone, with the draws held fixed.

```{julia}
md_table(["action", "expected newts alive", "standard error", "simulation only"],
         [[e.action, Float64(e.value), e.standard_error, e.simulation_error]
          for e in expected_utility_estimates(problem)])
```

The actions are close, and the standard errors are large beside the differences. That
comparison is misleading, because the three actions were run on the same draws with the
same random numbers. The right error for a difference is the error of the paired
difference. `payoff_table` with a `baseline` computes the gain of each action over no
intervention replicate by replicate:

```{julia}
gains = DecisionProblem(payoff_table(table, alive; baseline=:none), belief)
md_table(["action", "expected gain over no intervention", "standard error", "simulation only"],
         [[e.action, Float64(e.value), e.standard_error, e.simulation_error]
          for e in expected_utility_estimates(gains)])
```

Treatment gains about two newts on average, and the gain is several standard errors from
zero.

### Rules on a sample

The rules of the earlier vignettes apply unchanged. A sample is a single prior.

```{julia}
rules = ["expected utility" => MaxExpectedUtility(),
         "CVaR, worst 20%" => DecisionRule(CVaR(0.2)),
         "lower quartile" => DecisionRule(Quantile(0.25)), "maximin" => Maximin(),
         "minimax regret" => MinimaxRegret()]
md_table(["rule", "first choice", "score of the choice"],
         [[name, first_choice(decide(problem, rule)),
           Float64(decide(problem, rule).scores[findfirst(==(first_choice(decide(problem, rule))),
                                                          action_labels(problem))])]
          for (name, rule) in rules])
```

The worst case over a sample is the worst draw that happened to be sampled. A larger
sample can only make it worse. The result says so:

```{julia}
decide(problem, Maximin()).details.sample_note
```

Operations that have no meaning for a sample throw `BeliefFormError`. An unweighted
mean over draws ignores their weights:

```{julia}
try
    aggregate(Laplace(), problem)
catch err
    sprint(showerror, err)
end
```

### The weight on infected animals

The infection utility is uninfected − w × infected. Expected utility is linear in w, so
the values of w at which the choice changes are found exactly, not on a grid.

```{julia}
uninfected = individuals_payoff(table, :uninfected)
infected = individuals_payoff(table, :infected)
base = DecisionProblem(uninfected, belief; baseline=:none)
regions = policy_regions(base, -infected; from=0, to=3)
md_table(["from w", "to w", "best action"],
         [[Float64(r.from), Float64(r.to), r.actions] for r in regions])
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
sweep = weight_sweep(w -> DecisionProblem(table, InfectionUtility(; weight=w); baseline=:none),
                     0:0.25:3)
plt = Plots.plot(; xlabel="weight w on infected newts", ylabel="expected uninfected − w × infected",
                 title="Expected utility by action (illustrative)")
for (i, a) in enumerate(TOY_ACTIONS)
    Plots.plot!(plt, [row.weight for row in sweep], [Float64(row.scores[i]) for row in sweep];
                label=String(a))
end
png_figure(plt)
```

## Value of information from a sample

`evpi(problem)` applies the definition to the sample. Called with a method, `evpi`
returns the same number with its Monte Carlo error and its two selection biases beside
it, never folded in.

```{julia}
plain = evpi(problem, SampleAverage(); noise_correlation=crn_correlation(table, alive))
regression = evpi(problem, SplineRegression())
voi_table(["EVPI, plain sample average" => plain,
           "EVPI, all-parameter regression" => regression])
```

Two things bias the pieces of this calculation, and both are instances of the
optimiser's curse: a maximum of estimates overstates, on average, what the chosen
action is worth.

- The **act-now bias** is the upward bias of the best expected utility, from
  maximising over sample means. It belongs to the reported value of the chosen action.
- The **cell-noise bias** is the upward bias of the perfect-information value, from
  taking a maximum over noisy cells at every draw.

EVPI is the difference of two terms that are each biased upwards, so the sign of its
bias is not determined in general. The regression estimate replaces the noisy cells by
fitted conditional means given all the parameters, so the simulation noise is smoothed
and not maximised over. It is the estimate to prefer for a stochastic simulator.

The split of each action's variance says how much of the spread across cells is the
parameters and how much is the simulator:

```{julia}
md_table(["action", "total variance", "simulation", "parameter", "parameter share"],
         [[v.action, v.total, v.simulation, v.parameter, v.parameter_share]
          for v in variance_components(problem)])
```

Here almost all of the variance is between draws: twenty replicates are plenty. The
EVPI is about a newt and a half per pond, small beside the sixty or so that survive.
The next vignette asks which parameter that value sits in.

## The report

`DecisionReport` works for a sample-based problem and shows the Monte Carlo standard
errors beside every estimate.

```{julia}
DecisionReport(problem; parameters=[:contact, :habitat],
               noise_correlation=crn_correlation(table, alive))
```

## What to take away

- A `SampleBelief` holds draws of named parameters with weights. It is a single prior,
  and everything computed from it is an estimate.
- An `OutcomeTable` holds outcomes by draw × action × replicate. Build it with
  `outcomes` from a model that implements the four adapter verbs, or from any table of
  runs. Failed runs are kept and counted.
- `outcomes` uses common random numbers across actions; `crn_correlation` reports what
  they achieved.
- `payoff_table(outcomes, utility)` gives conditional expected utilities, with standard
  errors and replicate counts in separate fields. One run per cell is flagged.
- For a difference between actions use `payoff_table(...; baseline)`: its errors are
  those of the paired differences.
- `evpi(problem, method)` returns a `VOIEstimate`: value, standard error, and the two
  selection biases. With noisy cells, prefer the all-parameter regression.
- Selection bias belongs to the best reported value and the chosen action. The sign of
  the bias of EVPI is not determined.
